title: Build Grid Ref Rescue, a map game where you find and give grid references
kind: a game chapter: build one game from each pair, and this pair is chapters 16 and 18
one: You build Grid Ref Rescue in your own project, exactly as it is in Summit Ready, and test it. Then you change it into a grid game on your own topic.

stages.title: See what Grid Ref Rescue does and how a round plays

screens.title: Look at a round of Grid Ref Rescue, from the first radio message to the score

blocks.p: By the end of this screen, you will know how a round of Grid Ref Rescue plays and how it scores.
Grid Ref Rescue is a map game. It is on Chimney Rock Mountain, the sixth place on the Summit Ready map.
You build one game from each pair of game chapters. Grid Ref Rescue is paired with Listen Out, so you build one of those two.
First you build Grid Ref Rescue exactly as it is in Summit Ready. Then, in stage 5, you change it into a grid game on your own topic.
A map of the Mourne Mountains fills the left of the window. Blue lines cut it into 100 squares, 10 across and 10 down. Each square is 1 kilometre wide.
Numbers sit in the margins outside the map. Along the top, the columns read 27 to 36 from left to right. Down the left side, the rows read 31 at the top down to 22 at the bottom.
Each [[grid square|2]] has a name made of 4 numbers: the number above its column, then the number beside its row. These 4 numbers are the square's [[grid reference|3]].
So the square under 31 and beside 27 is square 3127. The number along the top always comes first.
A round has 5 [[rescues|1]]. Each one starts with a radio message in the white box on the right.
The first 3 rescues are find rescues. The radio message gives a grid reference, such as 3127, and you click that square on the map.
The last 2 rescues are tell rescues. A red pin sits somewhere on the map. You type the grid reference of the pin's square, then click **Send to the helicopter**.
A right answer on your first try scores 20 points. The helicopter sound plays, and the square turns green.
A wrong first try turns that square red, and the box under the button says how to read the map. A right answer on your second try scores 10 points.
A wrong second try scores 0 points for that rescue. The right square turns green, so you can see where it was.
If you type the right numbers the wrong way round, such as 2731 for 3127, the game says so. It still counts as a wrong try.
Typing something that is not 4 numbers costs nothing. Neither does a grid reference that is off the map. A message says what is wrong, and you try again.
After each rescue, **Next rescue** appears. After the 5th rescue, the button says **See my score**, and it opens the Round over box.
The best score is 5 rescues at 20 points each, which is 100 points. The flag on Chimney Rock Mountain gets a tick on the map.

box.title: How real maps number the squares

blocks.p: A real walking map numbers its grid lines, not its squares. A square takes the number of the line along its left edge, then the number of the line along its bottom edge.
Summit Ready puts each number in the middle of its column or its row. So you can read a square's name straight off the margins, without working out which line is which.
Both ways give a square the same kind of name: the number along the top first, then the number down the side.

words: return
`return` hands a value back to the code that called the method, and ends the method there.
rescue
One of the 5 radio messages in a round of Grid Ref Rescue. In the code, each one is a Rescue object.
grid square
One of the 100 squares on the map. Each square is 1 kilometre wide.
grid reference
The 4 numbers that name a grid square: the number along the top, then the number down the left side.
bin\Debug
The folder inside your project where Visual Studio 2019 puts the program it builds. Summit Ready reads its data, pictures and sounds from there.
zip file
One file with other files and folders packed inside it.
property
A named value that an object carries, such as `Square` on a Rescue. `{ get; set; }` lets other code read the value and change it.
constructor
A method with the same name as its class. It runs once, when code makes a new object with `new`.
static
A method marked `static` belongs to the class itself. You call it on the class name, as in `Rescue.LoadAll()`.
List
A list that grows as you add to it. `List<Rescue>` is a list that holds Rescue objects.
continue
Inside a loop, `continue` skips the rest of this turn of the loop. The loop goes straight on to its next turn.
lightning bolt
The button at the top of the Properties window that shows a control's events in place of its properties.
field
A variable written at the top of the class, outside every method. Every method in the form can use it, and it keeps its value until the window closes.
const
A value that never changes while the program runs. `const int KM = 56;` names the number 56 once, so the code says KM everywhere else.
array
A row of values of the same type, kept together under one name and numbered from 0. `lblCol[0]` is the first label, and `lblCol[9]` is the 10th label.
panel
A control that holds other controls. `pnlPlay` is the play area that holds the map and the 20 number labels.
colour from red, green and blue
`Color.FromArgb(62, 142, 65)` mixes a colour from red, green and blue. Each number is from 0 to 255.
see-through colour
With 4 numbers, `Color.FromArgb` puts how solid the colour is first. 0 is clear, 255 is solid, and 115 lets the map show through.
Controls.Add
Puts a control that code made onto a window or a panel. Until then, the control exists, but nobody can see it.
Substring
Gives part of some text. `"3127".Substring(0, 2)` starts at place 0 and takes 2 letters, which gives `"31"`.
int.Parse
Turns text made of digits into a whole number, so that `"31"` becomes the number 31.
null
`null` means that a variable holds no object yet. `pin` holds `null` until the first tell rescue makes a pin.
Dispose
Takes a control off the screen for good, and frees what it used.
Paint
The event a control has when Windows draws it. Code in its handler draws on top of the control.
Graphics
The drawing surface that the Paint event gives you, as `e.Graphics`. Its methods draw lines and shapes.
Pen
What DrawLine draws with: a colour, and how wide the line is.
DrawLine
Draws a straight line from one point to another, with a Pen.
FillRectangle
Fills a box with a colour, given its left edge, its top edge, its width and its height.
Invalidate
Tells a control that its picture is out of date. Windows then runs its Paint event again.
MouseClick
The event a control has when you click it with the mouse. It also says where the click was.
MouseEventArgs
The kind of information that `e` holds when a mouse event runs. It says where the mouse was and which button was pressed.
e.X and e.Y
How far the click was from the left edge and from the top edge of the control, in pixels.
whole-number division
`/` between two whole numbers drops anything after the decimal point. `130 / 56` is 2, not 2.32.
Trim
Gives a copy of some text with any spaces at the start and the end taken off.
try and catch
Code inside `try` runs. If it throws an exception, the matching `catch` runs, and the program does not crash.
throw
`throw` stops a method and hands an exception back to the code that called it.
char.IsDigit
Says whether one letter of some text is a digit, from 0 to 9.
or
`||` means or. The `if` is true when any one of its parts is true.
event
Something that happens to a control, such as a click on a button.
handler
The method that runs when an event happens. `btnSend_Click` is the handler for a click on **Send to the helicopter**.
AddRange
`AddRange` adds every item from one list to the end of another list, in one go.
Height
How tall a control or a picture is, in pixels.
red underline
The wavy red line Visual Studio 2019 draws under code it does not understand yet. Often it means a method you have not written yet.

box.title: If a file is missing or broken

blocks.p: Grid Ref Rescue never crashes because a file is missing. This is what you see instead.
If `rescues.txt` is missing, or has fewer than 3 find lines or 2 tell lines, the radio message box says **Grid Ref Rescue needs 3 find and 2 tell rescues in Data\rescues.txt.**
If a line of `rescues.txt` does not have exactly 3 parts, Grid Ref Rescue skips that line.
If `mournes-grid-600.png` is missing, the grid lines and the numbers still show, on a plain background.
If a sound is missing, that moment is silent, and the game carries on.
To put a missing file back, you download the [[zip file|5]] again and paste its folders into bin\Debug. When Windows asks about the files you already have, you click **Skip these files**.
Skipping keeps every file you already have, including any file you changed. Only the missing files are copied in.

code.title: Rescue.cs: the Rescue class
code.why: You type the 3 properties, and the 3 lines that put a value into each one, because they are new. The rest reads a file the same way as `LoadAll` in chapter 3, so it comes in the copy.
partLines: The class and its 3 properties

`class Rescue` starts the class. Each property holds one part of a line of `rescues.txt`. `Kind` holds find or tell. `Square` holds the grid square, such as 3127. `Message` holds the radio message. `{ get; set; }` lets other code read each property and change it.
The constructor

This part is the constructor. It runs when code writes `new Rescue(parts)`. `parts` is one line of `rescues.txt`, already cut into 3 pieces at each bar. The constructor puts `parts[0]` into `Kind`, `parts[1]` into `Square` and `parts[2]` into `Message`.
The start of LoadAll

`static` means that you call LoadAll on the class itself, as `Rescue.LoadAll()`. You do not need a Rescue object first. LoadAll starts with an empty list. `Files.Data` from chapter 2 gives the full path of `rescues.txt` in the Data folder. If `rescues.txt` is not there, LoadAll hands back the empty list, so the game shows a message and does not crash.
Read every line

The StreamReader is the tool that reads a file one line at a time. It opens `rescues.txt`. The loop goes round once for each line, until the end of the file. `Split('|')` cuts each line at each bar into `parts`. If a line does not have exactly 3 parts, `continue` skips it and the loop moves on to the next line. Every good line becomes a new Rescue, and `rescues.Add` puts it on the end of the list.
Close the file and hand back the list
`reader.Close()` closes `rescues.txt`, so that other programs can open it again. `return rescues;` hands the full list back to the code that called LoadAll.

screens.title: Type the Grid Ref Rescue fields

blocks.p: By the end of this screen, frmGridRef has the variables that remember the rescues, the tries and the coloured squares.
These variables are called [[fields|12]]. They sit at the top of the class, outside every method, so every method in the form can use them.
Every field below is new in this chapter, so you type every one. There are 17 of them, so they come in 2 groups.

code.title: The Grid Ref Rescue fields, first group
code.text:
// ---------- Grid Ref Rescue ----------
const int KM = 56;                     // pixels in 1 km on the map
private List<Rescue> plays = new List<Rescue>();   // the 5 rescues
private int number = 0;                // this rescue, 0 to 4
private int tries = 0;                 // tries on this rescue
private bool rescueDone = false;       // true once right or shown
private int total = 0;                 // points from every rescue
private List<string> squares = new List<string>();  // to colour in
private List<bool> good = new List<bool>();      // green or red
partLines: Pixels in 1 kilometre
Each grid square on the map is 56 pixels wide, and stands for 1 kilometre. `const` means that KM never changes. The code says KM wherever it needs 56.
The 5 rescues
`plays` holds the 5 rescues of this round, in the order they are played.
The state of a rescue
`number` is this rescue, from 0 to 4. `tries` counts the tries on this rescue. `rescueDone` turns true once the rescue is right, or the answer is shown. `total` adds up the points from every rescue.
The squares to colour in
`squares` holds every square the map colours in on this rescue, such as `"3127"`. `good` holds true for a green square and false for a red one, in the same order.

code.title: The Grid Ref Rescue fields, second group
partLines: The 2 arrays of number labels

The drawing colours

`gridPen` draws the blue grid lines. `goodBrush` fills a green square, and `badBrush` fills a red square. Each colour has 4 numbers: how solid it is, then red, green and blue. Below 255, the map shows through the colour.

screens.title: Type MakeNumbers, which puts the 20 numbers in the margins

blocks.p: By the end of this screen, frmGridRef can make the 20 numbers in the margins of the map.
20 labels would take a long time to drop by hand. A for loop makes them in code: it goes round 10 times, and each time it makes one top label and one side label.
Each column is 56 pixels wide, and the map starts 48 pixels in from the left of pnlPlay. So the label for column `c` starts at 48 plus 56 for each column before it.
The top number of column `c` is 27 plus `c`, so the numbers run from 27 to 36. The side number of row `c` is 31 minus `c`, so the numbers run from 31 down to 22.

box.title: Where the labels for column 2 and row 2 go

blocks.p: The top label for `c` = 2 starts at 48 + 2 × 56, which is 160 pixels in. It reads 27 + 2, which is 29.
The side label for `c` = 2 starts at 32 + 2 × 56, which is 144 pixels down. It reads 31 - 2, which is 29.

code.title: MakeNumbers
code.why: The 11 lines for `lblRow[c]` repeat the 11 lines for `lblCol[c]` with 4 numbers changed, so those 11 lines come in the copy.
partLines: A new Label for each column
The loop goes round 10 times, with `c` from 0 to 9. `new Label()` makes a new Label, and `lblCol[c]` keeps it in the array.
How the top label looks
Each line sets one property, as you set them in the Properties window. The label is as wide as one column, and its number sits in its middle, in bold.
Put the label on pnlPlay
`pnlPlay.Controls.Add` puts the new label on pnlPlay, so it shows.
The side label
The side label is made in the same way. It is 36 pixels wide and as tall as one row, and it reads 31 minus `c`.

blocks.p: By the end of this screen, frmGridRef can put the red pin at a random spot inside any grid square.
MakePin works out where the square is on the map from its 4 numbers. The first 2 numbers give the column, and the last 2 give the row.
`square.Substring(0, 2)` takes the first 2 digits, such as `"31"`. `int.Parse` turns that text into the number 31.

box.title: Where square 3127 is on the map, in words first

blocks.p: The column is the top number minus 27. For 3127 that is 31 - 27, which is column 4.
The row is 31 minus the side number. For 3127 that is 31 - 27, which is row 4.
Each square is 56 pixels wide, so the square's left edge is 4 × 56, which is 224 pixels in. Its top edge is 4 × 56, which is 224 pixels down.
In the code, that is `(top - 27) * KM` and `(31 - side) * KM`.

code.title: MakePin
partLines: The 2 numbers

The pin starts at the square's left edge and top edge, plus a few pixels. `random.Next(18)` adds 0 to 17 more pixels, so the pin sits in a slightly different spot each time.

`picMap.Controls.Add(pin)` puts the pin on the map itself, so its Left and Top count from the map's corner.

box.title: What Paint draws, in words first

blocks.p: For each square in the list `squares`: work out its left edge and top edge, in the same way as MakePin. Fill a box 56 pixels wide and 56 pixels tall there, green if it was right and red if it was wrong.

partLines: The drawing surface

The [[MouseClick|29]] event says where the click was, in pixels from the map's top left corner. `[[e.X|31]]` is how far in from the left. `e.Y` is how far down from the top.

box.title: A click at 130 pixels in and 250 pixels down, in words first

blocks.p: The column is how many whole squares fit before the click: 130 ÷ 56 is 2, with some left over. So the click is in column 2.
The row works the same way: 250 ÷ 56 is 4, with some left over. So the click is in row 4.
The top number is 27 + 2, which is 29. The side number is 31 - 4, which is 27. So the square is 2927.
In C#, `/` between 2 whole numbers drops what is left over. This is [[whole-number division|32]], so `e.X / KM` gives the column straight away.

code.title: picMap_MouseClick
partLines: Clicks that do nothing

The top number and the side number are turned into text and joined, such as `"29"` and `"27"` into `"2927"`. `Judge` marks the answer. `false` says that it came from a click, not from typing.

stages.title: Change Grid Ref Rescue into a game on your own topic

screens.title: Choose your own grid, and 2 more things to change

blocks.p: By the end of this screen, you have chosen your own grid and 2 more things to change.

Your own game keeps the Grid Ref Rescue code, but uses your own topic. Any topic with a picture cut into 10 columns and 10 rows works. The numbers along the top and down the side must each have 2 digits, such as 10 to 19. A grid reference is then 4 digits long.
Maths: a grid of coordinates. The player finds a point from its x and y numbers, or types the numbers of a marked point.
Chemistry: the first 100 elements, 10 to a row. The player finds an element from its column and row numbers.
Geography: a street map of your town. The player finds a building from its grid reference.

Change at least 2 more things as well, so that your game plays differently from Grid Ref Rescue. For example, change the points, the number of tries, the colours of the squares or the number of rescues.
Every picture and sound you use must be free to use. Each one gets a line in `credits.txt`, saying who made it, its licence and a link.

blocks.p: By the end of this screen, your game reads your own data file and shows your own grid picture.
Your own files go in the same folders as the Summit Ready files, inside bin\Debug. Your data file goes in Data, and your grid picture goes in a folder inside Images.
Your picture must be square, so that it fits the map box `picMap` without stretching. Make it 560 pixels wide, or 1120, which shrinks to 560 evenly.

Change `rescues.txt` in LoadAll to the name of your text file.

Change `"Map"` and `"mournes-grid-600.png"` in frmGridRef_Load to your folder and your picture.

glossary: return
`return` hands a value back to the code that called the method, and ends the method there.
rescue
One of the 5 radio messages in a round of Grid Ref Rescue. In the code, each one is a Rescue object.
grid square
One of the 100 squares on the map. Each square is 1 kilometre wide.
grid reference
The 4 numbers that name a grid square: the number along the top, then the number down the left side.
bin\Debug
The folder inside your project where Visual Studio 2019 puts the program it builds. Summit Ready reads its data, pictures and sounds from there.
zip file
One file with other files and folders packed inside it.
property
A named value that an object carries, such as `Square` on a Rescue. `{ get; set; }` lets other code read the value and change it.
constructor
A method with the same name as its class. It runs once, when code makes a new object with `new`.
static
A method marked `static` belongs to the class itself. You call it on the class name, as in `Rescue.LoadAll()`.
List
A list that grows as you add to it. `List<Rescue>` is a list that holds Rescue objects.
continue
Inside a loop, `continue` skips the rest of this turn of the loop. The loop goes straight on to its next turn.
lightning bolt
The button at the top of the Properties window that shows a control's events in place of its properties.
field
A variable written at the top of the class, outside every method. Every method in the form can use it, and it keeps its value until the window closes.
const
A value that never changes while the program runs. `const int KM = 56;` names the number 56 once, so the code says KM everywhere else.
array
A row of values of the same type, kept together under one name and numbered from 0. `lblCol[0]` is the first label, and `lblCol[9]` is the 10th label.
panel
A control that holds other controls. `pnlPlay` is the play area that holds the map and the 20 number labels.
colour from red, green and blue
`Color.FromArgb(62, 142, 65)` mixes a colour from red, green and blue. Each number is from 0 to 255.
see-through colour
With 4 numbers, `Color.FromArgb` puts how solid the colour is first. 0 is clear, 255 is solid, and 115 lets the map show through.
Controls.Add
Puts a control that code made onto a window or a panel. Until then, the control exists, but nobody can see it.
Substring
Gives part of some text. `"3127".Substring(0, 2)` starts at place 0 and takes 2 letters, which gives `"31"`.
int.Parse
Turns text made of digits into a whole number, so that `"31"` becomes the number 31.
null
`null` means that a variable holds no object yet. `pin` holds `null` until the first tell rescue makes a pin.
Dispose
Takes a control off the screen for good, and frees what it used.
Paint
The event a control has when Windows draws it. Code in its handler draws on top of the control.
Graphics
The drawing surface that the Paint event gives you, as `e.Graphics`. Its methods draw lines and shapes.
Pen
What DrawLine draws with: a colour, and how wide the line is.
DrawLine
Draws a straight line from one point to another, with a Pen.
FillRectangle
Fills a box with a colour, given its left edge, its top edge, its width and its height.
Invalidate
Tells a control that its picture is out of date. Windows then runs its Paint event again.
MouseClick
The event a control has when you click it with the mouse. It also says where the click was.
MouseEventArgs
The kind of information that `e` holds when a mouse event runs. It says where the mouse was and which button was pressed.
e.X and e.Y
How far the click was from the left edge and from the top edge of the control, in pixels.
whole-number division
`/` between two whole numbers drops anything after the decimal point. `130 / 56` is 2, not 2.32.
Trim
Gives a copy of some text with any spaces at the start and the end taken off.
try and catch
Code inside `try` runs. If it throws an exception, the matching `catch` runs, and the program does not crash.
throw
`throw` stops a method and hands an exception back to the code that called it.
char.IsDigit
Says whether one letter of some text is a digit, from 0 to 9.
or
`||` means or. The `if` is true when any one of its parts is true.
event
Something that happens to a control, such as a click on a button.
handler
The method that runs when an event happens. `btnSend_Click` is the handler for a click on **Send to the helicopter**.
AddRange
`AddRange` adds every item from one list to the end of another list, in one go.
Height
How tall a control or a picture is, in pixels.
red underline
The wavy red line Visual Studio 2019 draws under code it does not understand yet. Often it means a method you have not written yet.
